The 19th Amendment was ratified on this day in 1920, granting women across the country the right to vote.

That didn't mean the suffrage movement was over, though.

A century later, widespread voter suppression and felony laws mean that many people still are not guaranteed access to the ballot box.

#TheMarchContinues #VotingRights | Civil Rights Memorial | Facebook

The "Good Trouble Quilts" exhibit is on display at the Civil Rights Memorial Center until May 1.Civil Rights Memorial950 views · March 25, 20250:31#OTD in 1955, sparked by the arrest of Rosa Parks four days earlier, the Montgomery, Alabama, Bus Boycott began. It was a 13-month mass protest of racial segregation, the first of its scale in the nation. The Montgomery Improvement Association coordinated the boycott under the leadership of Martin Luther King Jr. To sustain the effort, Black leaders organized carpools, and the city’s Black taxi drivers charged the same price as bus fare for Black riders. On Dec. 21, 1956, the boycott ended, and the buses were integrated. #TheMarchContinuesCivil Rights Memorial371 views · December 5, 20240:48#OTD, President Abraham Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation. He said the “paramount object in the struggle is to save the Union, and is not either to save or destroy slavery.” The proclamation freed approximately 3 million of the 4.1 million enslaved people. Not until the 13th Amendment was ratified was slavery abolished in the entire nation. Though slavery was technically outlawed, it quickly morphed into new forms of oppression.
